  638: \begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray characterization]
  639:   \label{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
  640:   For a canonical eventually recurrent numeration system satisfying
  641:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, the following are equivalent.
  642:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  643:     \item There are a finite \(k\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
  644:     \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
  645:     \[
  646:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty.
  647:     \]
  648:     \item The system admits a geometric synchronized scheme in the
  649:     sense of \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}.
  650:     \item The language \(\mathcal R_U\) contains an infinite linear MCFL
  651:     \(L_0=\{W(t):t\ge0\}\) of finite fan-out for which there are
  652:     \(c\ge1,b\ge2\) satisfying
  653:     \[
  654:       \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\qquad(t\ge0).
  655:     \]
  656:   \end{enumerate}
  657: \end{theorem}
  658: 
  659: \begin{proof}
  660:   Suppose first that \textup{(i)} holds. Use the minimal tail recurrence
  661:   as the witness in
  662:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, and write its resulting
  663:   ray and strictly increasing value sequence as \(W(t)\) and \(N(t)\).
  664:   Let
  665:   \[
  666:     K_0=\max_{t\ge0}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(N(t)),
  667:   \]
  668:   and choose \(t_0\) attaining the maximum. Let \(T\) be the set of
  669:   primes outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\) that divide \(N(t_0)\), and put
  670:   \(q=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\). If \(T\ne\varnothing\), take the return
  671:   time \(H=H(q)\) from
  672:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}; if \(T=\varnothing\),
  673:   put \(H=1\). Every prime in \(T\) divides every \(N(t_0+nH)\). A prime
  674:   divisor outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\) would therefore give at least
  675:   \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary
  676:   to the definition of \(K_0\). Thus all terms of
  677:   \[
  678:     Y(n)=N(t_0+nH)
  679:   \]
  680:   are supported on the fixed finite set \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\).
  681: 
  682:   The entries of every matrix power \(M^n\) satisfy a linear recurrence
  683:   by Cayley--Hamilton. The expression for \(N(t)\) is a finite sum of
  684:   finite products of such entries, and linear recurrence sequences are
  685:   closed under sums and termwise products. Hence \(Y\) is a strictly
  686:   increasing positive integer recurrence. By
  687:   \Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}, there are
  688:   \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1,b\ge2\) such that
  689:   \(N(t_\ast+h_\ast n)=cb^n\), where
  690:   \(t_\ast=t_0+Hr\) and \(h_\ast=Hh\).
  691: 
  692:   In the synchronized factorization, replace
  693:   \[
  694:     u_j\ \text{by}\ u_jv_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  695:     v_j\ \text{by}\ v_j^{h_\ast},\qquad
  696:     w_j\ \text{by}\ w_js_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  697:     s_j\ \text{by}\ s_j^{h_\ast}.
  698:   \]
  699:   This absorbs the fixed powers and parametrizes exactly the subray
  700:   \(W(t_\ast+h_\ast n)\). Its total pumped length remains positive, so
  701:   it is a geometric synchronized scheme. This proves
  702:   \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.
  703: 
  704:   The implication \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)} is
  705:   \Cref{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}. Finally, under
  706:   \textup{(iii)}, the language \(L_0\) is an infinite MCFL and
  707:   \[
  708:     \omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(cb^t)\le\omega(cb)
  709:     \qquad(t\ge0),
  710:   \]
  711:   proving \textup{(i)}.
  712: \end{proof}
  713: 
  714: \begin{corollary}[Positive semidecidability]
  715:   \label{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}
  716:   Suppose the numeration system is given effectively by its finite
  717:   digit alphabet, recurrence and initial data, and a DFA recognizing
  718:   \(\mathcal R_U\), with the minimal tail recurrence and a valid
  719:   threshold \(J_{\mathrm r}\) effectively computable from these data.
  720:   Then the property in
  721:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}\textup{(i)} is
  722:   recursively enumerable, equivalently it has a \(\Sigma^0_1\) upper
  723:   bound.
  724: \end{corollary}
  725: 
  726: \begin{proof}
  727:   Enumerate \(k\ge1\), \(a\in A^{J_{\mathrm r}}\), and all finite tuples
  728:   of words occurring in
  729:   \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}, rejecting tuples of zero
  730:   total pumped length. For a fixed tuple, whether the DFA accepts
  731:   \(W(t)\) for every \(t\ge0\) is decidable: the tuple of powers of the
  732:   finitely many pumped-block transformations is eventually periodic in
  733:   the finite transition monoid, and its preperiod and period are found
  734:   by exhaustive iteration.
  735: 
  736:   The affine matrices construct an exact linear recurrence for
  737:   \[
  738:     N(t)=\val_U(W(t)).
  739:   \]
  740:   Kronecker products implement the termwise
  741:   products arising from the several synchronized block powers. For a
  742:   tuple accepted at every parameter, compute \(c=N(0)\). The only
  743:   possible integer ratio is \(b=N(1)/N(0)\). Check that
  744:   \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\), and then decide whether the recurrence
  745:   \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero by checking an initial segment of
  746:   length equal to an explicitly constructed recurrence order. Thus each
  747:   candidate scheme is decidable, and the enumeration halts exactly on
  748:   positive instances by
  749:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}. No claim of a
  750:   decision procedure for negative instances is made.
  751: \end{proof}
  752: 
  753: \begin{theorem}[Arbitrarily deep quotient congruences]
  754:   \label{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}
  755:   Suppose \(\abs{a_0}=1\), and let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an
  756:   infinite MCFL. For arbitrary sequences \(M_i\ge1\) and \(r_i\ge1\),
  757:   \(L\) contains a strictly increasing sequence \(N_i\) such that
  758:   \[
  759:     N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
  760:     Q_i\equiv1\pmod {M_iN_i^{r_i}}.
  761:   \]

 succeeded in 185ms:
  181:   N_L(T):=\#\{w\in L:\val(w)\le T\},
  182: \]
  183: where \(\val(w)\) is the Zeckendorf value of \(w\). The growth law says
  184: \[
  185:   N_L(T)=T^{\alpha+o(1)},
  186:   \qquad
  187:   \alpha=
  188:   \begin{cases}
  189:     0, & \rho\le 1,\\[0.3em]
  190:     \dfrac{\log \rho}{\log \varphi}, & \rho>1.
  191:   \end{cases}
  192:   \qquad (T\to\infty).
  193: \]
  194: \Cref{sec:zeckendorf} combines this background statement with
  195: prime-counting estimates to deduce the quantitative Zeckendorf
  196: slice-obstruction corollaries. Its language-theoretic conclusions are
  197: stronger and do not use the prime number theorem. The regular theorem
  198: \Cref{thm:coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping} and its context-free
  199: extension
  200: \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping} prove, by
  201: block-action pumping modulo \(N_i^2\), that every sufficiently long
  202: word in the respective language class starts an infinite chain
  203: \[
  204:   N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}.
  205: \]
  206: Thus each pumping step may be chosen with quotient coprime to the
  207: previous value, and \(\omega(\val(w))\) is unbounded on every infinite
  208: context-free \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\). The general recurrent-system
  209: results
  210: \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit,thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint,thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy,thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
  211: upgrade prime immunity to MCF-immunity and isolate the exact nonunit
  212: escape alternative and its intrinsic geometric-ray inverse. The
  213: positive semidecidability consequence is
  214: \Cref{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}. In unit systems,
  215: \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain,thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}
  216: give arbitrary congruence depth and the induced divisibility tree.
  217: The specialization to standard linear Pisot \(U\)-systems is
  218: \Cref{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}. In the endpoint case \(\rho\le1\), the
  219: displayed formula is used only in the form \(N_L(T)=T^{o(1)}\).
  220: 
  221: \begin{example}[LSD-first Zeckendorf convention]\label{ex:lsd-zeck}
  222:   Consider the integer \(23=F_8+F_3\). Its Zeckendorf expansion uses
  223:   digits \(x_k\in\{0,1\}\) with \(x_k\) multiplying \(F_{k+1}\) and the
  224:   least significant digit listed first. The admissible word
  225:   \(w=0100001\) has length \(7\), satisfies the no-\(11\) rule, and
  226:   evaluates to
  227:   \(x_1F_2+x_2F_3+\cdots+x_7F_8=0+1\cdot 2+\cdots+1\cdot 21=23\).
  228:   The terminal \(1\) is the most significant digit, consistent with the
  229:   trim deterministic presentation used in \Cref{sec:zeckendorf}.
  230: \end{example}
  231: 
  232: The final remarks are only contextual. They recall the classical
  233: P\'olya--Carlson--Estermann natural-boundary obstruction for
  234: prime-supported Euler products and the elementary \(2\pi i\)-periodicity
  235: of scalar determinant models after \(z=e^{-s}\); these statements are
  236: not used in the finite-budget proofs.
  237: 
  238: \subsection{Relation to prior work}\label{subsec:prior-work}
  239: 
  240: We give a theorem-by-theorem account of what is known, what is a
  241: specialized reproof, and what is new.
  242: 
  243: \begin{itemize}
  244:   \item \textbf{\suppref{Theorem~1.2} (density dichotomy):
  245:   classical.} The eventual periodicity of normalized word counts for a
  246:   deterministic automaton is a direct Perron--Frobenius consequence and
  247:   is standard in the density literature for regular languages; see
  248:   \cite{Berstel1973,SalomaaSoittola1978,BodirskyGaertnerVonOertzenSchwinghammer2004,Bell2020UpperDensity,Koga2019Density,BerstelReutenauer2011}.
  249:   We record it only in the residue-class form needed for the later
  250:   prime estimates.
  251: 
  252:   \item \textbf{\suppref{Lemma~1.16} and
  253:   \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-powerlaw}: classical.} These results are standard residue-class regroupings of
  254:   the periodic Perron--Frobenius theorem for trim strongly connected
  255:   presentations and of the known Zeckendorf growth law; see, e.g.,
  256:   \cite{SalomaaSoittola1978,LecomteRigo2001,CharlierRampersad2011}.
  257: 
  258:   \item \textbf{Multicomponent theorem.}
  259:   \suppref{Theorem~1.14} keeps the
  260:   residue-wise exponential-polynomial expansion on the Perron-scale
  261:   active classes of arbitrary trim deterministic presentations, absorbs
  262:   lower-growth classes into the sub-Perron term, and compares the
  263:   polynomial exponents in the product automaton. This is the
  264:   presentation-level finite-budget result used to handle maximal
  265:   components connected by transient paths.
  266: 
  267:   \item \textbf{\suppref{Theorem~1.18} (trim strongly connected
  268:   presentations).} This is the \(s_r=0\) specialization of the
  269:   multicomponent picture and agrees with the conditional-density
  270:   literature
  271:   \cite{HanselPerrin1989,Kozik2005Conditional,Koga2019Density,Montoya2025Relative,BertheGouletPerrin2025}.
  272:   Its role is to isolate the constants used in the Zeckendorf
  273:   application.
  274: 
  275:   \item \textbf{Effective quantitative prime-slice obstructions.} The
  276:   introductory binary corollaries above summarize the later statements
  277:   \suppref{Proposition~1.9}, \suppref{Corollary~1.10}, and
  278:   \suppref{Corollary~1.12}.
  279:   The effective theorem \suppref{Theorem~1.7}
  280:   makes the fixed-base constants and thresholds computable from a
  281:   compressed Markov-chain certificate for the transition matrix of the
  282:   given DFA. This is an effective packaging of the classical density
  283:   dichotomy with explicit prime-counting input, not a new density
  284:   dichotomy. Together with
  285:   \suppref{Corollary~1.19}, this gives a uniform
  286:   obstruction to approximating the base-\(b\) prime slices by a single
  287:   fixed DFA, both for symmetric difference and for simultaneous
  288:   recall/precision. The Zeckendorf analogues
  289:   \Cref{cor:zeck-symmetric-diff,cor:zeck-recall-precision} follow by the
  290:   same mechanism.
  291: 
  292:   \item \textbf{Coprime-quotient Zeckendorf pumping
  293:   (\Cref{thm:coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}).} The PNT-free
  294:   unimodular block-action argument is the primary new Zeckendorf
  295:   language theorem in this note. It uses
  296:   \Cref{lem:zeckendorf-unimodular-block-action,lem:zeckendorf-pumping-congruence}
  297:   with modulus \(N_i^2\) to build an infinite chain
  298:   \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\) inside any
  299:   infinite regular \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\). This implies that new
  300:   rational prime divisors occur along the chain, hence
  301:   \[
  302:     \sup_{w\in L}\omega(\val(w))=\infty.
  303:   \]
  304:   The bounded-distinct-prime and finite-prime-support REG-immunity
  305:   corollaries are the main language-theoretic consequences; bounded
  306:   almost-prime and prime-language REG-immunity are weaker downstream
  307:   cases. The slice-rigidity statement
  308:   \(\Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-slice-rigidity}\) remains a separate
  309:   density-scale obstruction, while the nonregularity corollary
  310:   \(\Cref{cor:zeckendorf-prime-language-not-regular}\) follows
  311:   immediately from REG-immunity. The sofic-slice exclusion
  312:   \(\Cref{rem:zeckendorf-primes-not-sofic}\) is then a short consequence
  313:   of regularity of sofic block languages.
  314: 
  315:   \item \textbf{Context-free, MCFL, and Pisot extensions.}
  316:   Fixed-base prime CF-immunity is classical. Hartmanis and Shank proved
  317:   that no infinite set of primes can be accepted in fixed-base notation
  318:   by a pushdown automaton; Sch\"utzenberger obtained the conclusion
  319:   independently \cite{HartmanisShank1968,Schutzenberger1968}. We do not
  320:   reproduce their proofs as new. Our use of Ogden's lemma
  321:   \cite{Ogden1968} instead couples the two pumped blocks to the
  322:   Zeckendorf unimodular action and yields the stronger coprime-quotient
  323:   chain
  324:   \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. The
  325:   weak pumping lemma of Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami
  326:   \cite{SekiEtAl1991} supplies one synchronized \(2k\)-block orbit for
  327:   every infinite \(k\)-MCFL; it is used as an input, not reproved.
  328:   Kanazawa--Kobele--Michaelis--Salvati--Yoshinaka prove that the usual
  329:   strong pumping form fails in general
  330:   \cite{KanazawaKobeleMichaelisSalvatiYoshinaka2014}, and the recent
  331:   substitution lemma of Duncan--Elder--Frenkel--Liu gives a different
  332:   strong interface \cite{DuncanElderFrenkelLiu2026}. Neither result
  333:   concerns recurrence numeration or divisibility. The new deductions
  334:   are the fixed local-congruence orbit
  335:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, the topological
  336:   fingerprint \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}, the exact rank
  337:   formula \Cref{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}, and the escape
  338:   dichotomy \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}. The unit-system
  339:   constructions are \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} and
  340:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}.
  341:   Evertse's theorem on prime ideals in ratios of terms of
  342:   nondegenerate recurrences \cite{Evertse1984} is used as an arithmetic
  343:   input to the geometric-ray characterization
  344:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}; it is not claimed as
  345:   a new recurrence theorem.
  346:   Broughan's \(\mathbb Q\)- and Cantor-space classifications for adic
  347:   integer topologies are cited as classical inputs
  348:   \cite{Broughan2003}. Frougny normalization and the
  349:   Bertrand/substitution literature
  350:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}
  351:   supply the canonical finite-state numeration interface, not the
  352:   arithmetic pumping proof. The residual nonunit and non-positional
  353:   limits are stated in \Cref{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}. The
  354:   recurrence-witness separation
  355:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation} distinguishes the invariant
  356:   minimal action from an arbitrarily inflated companion presentation.
  357: 
  358:   \item \textbf{Analytic obstructions: classical background.}
  359:   \suppref{Theorem~A.1} is the usual
  360:   P\'olya--Carlson natural-boundary mechanism for Euler products.
  361:   \suppref{Proposition~A.2} is the corresponding
  362:   periodicity obstruction for determinant models after \(z=e^{-s}\). Both are
  363:   classical
  364:   \cite{Polya1923,Carlson1921,Estermann1928,ArtinMazur1965,BowenLanford1970}.
  365: \end{itemize}
  366: \smallskip
  367: \noindent\textbf{Relation to density and approximation literature.} For ordinary
  368: automatic sets, asymptotic density questions go back at least to
  369: Berstel \cite{Berstel1973}; the standard global sources include
  370: B\"uchi's automata-theoretic decidability work \cite{Buchi1960} and
  371: Allouche--Shallit's monograph on automatic sequences
  372: \cite{AlloucheShallit2003}. Matrix and algorithmic treatments appear
  373: in
  374: \cite{BodirskyGaertnerVonOertzenSchwinghammer2004,Bell2020UpperDensity},
  375: and Koga's paper \cite{Koga2019Density} revisits Sin'ya's density-zero
  376: criterion \cite{Sinya2021}. The rational-measure viewpoint of Hansel
  377: and Perrin \cite{HanselPerrin1989} interprets regular languages via
  378: probability measures on shifts of finite type. Kozik's MFCS 2005 paper
  379: \cite{Kozik2005Conditional} formulates conditional densities for
  380: deterministic presentations in the trim strongly connected setting,
  381: Montoya \cite{Montoya2025Relative} recasts these questions in terms of
  382: relative densities, and Berth\'e--Goulet-Ouellet--Perrin
  383: \cite{BertheGouletPerrin2025} establish a broad density theorem under
  384: shift-invariant measures. Accordingly,
  385: \suppref{Theorem~1.2}, \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-powerlaw}, and
  386: \suppref{Theorem~1.18}
  387: should be read here as background statements in a form suited to the
  388: prime-slice applications, while
  389: \suppref{Theorem~1.14} is the exponent-sensitive
  390: extension needed for general trim deterministic presentations. Cobham's
  391: theorem
  392: \cite{Cobham1969} is the foundational reference for base-dependent
  393: automatic recognizability of sets of integers. Regular approximation of
  394: non-regular languages is a separate line of work; see, for example,
  395: Eisman and Ravikumar \cite{EismanRavikumar2005} and the asymptotic
  396: approximation framework of Sin'ya \cite{Sinya2021}. Polynomial and
  397: sparse growth phenomena for regular languages are part of the classical
  398: transfer-matrix picture \cite{Berstel1973,SalomaaSoittola1978}, and
  399: numeration systems on regular languages are treated in
  400: \cite{LecomteRigo2001,Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,CharlierRampersad2011,Rigo2014Vol1,Rigo2014Vol2}.
  401: The present contribution is narrower: it packages the fixed-DFA
  402: prime-slice obstruction with computable residue-class constants and
  403: explicit thresholds, then applies the same finite-budget argument in the
  404: Zeckendorf setting.
  405: 
  406: 
  407: \medskip
  408: \noindent\textbf{Summary.} \suppref{Theorem~1.2 and Lemma~1.16} and
  409: \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-powerlaw}
  410: record the density statements needed for deterministic presentations.
  411: \suppref{Theorem~1.14} gives the general trim
  412: deterministic finite-budget theorem, including multiple maximal
  413: components, Perron-active residue classes, and their polynomial factors,
  414: and \suppref{Theorem~1.18} records the strongly connected
  415: specialization used for Zeckendorf. The paper's effective contribution
  416: is the finite-budget obstruction mechanism with quantitative fixed-DFA
  417: recall/precision and symmetric-difference instances; see
  418: \suppref{Corollary~1.19}, \suppref{Proposition~1.9},
  419: \suppref{Corollary~1.10}, and \suppref{Corollary~1.12}.
  420: The Zeckendorf analogues are
  421: \Cref{cor:zeck-symmetric-diff,cor:zeck-recall-precision}. The
  422: Zeckendorf prime-language theorem is downstream of the PNT-free
  423: coprime-quotient pumping theorem
  424: \Cref{thm:coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. Its principal
  425: consequences are
  426: \Cref{cor:unbounded-distinct-prime-divisors,cor:bounded-distinct-prime-zeckendorf-languages-reg-immune}
  427: and \Cref{cor:finite-prime-support-zeckendorf-languages-reg-immune};
  428: \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-slice-rigidity} remains a separate
  429: slice-cardinality obstruction, and
  430: \Cref{cor:zeckendorf-prime-language-not-regular} is an immediate
  431: consequence of REG-immunity.
  432: Context-free Zeckendorf pumping is
  433: \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}, with the
  434: immunity consequences in
  435: \Cref{cor:zeckendorf-context-free-immunity-package}. The stronger MCFL
  436: package is
  437: \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit,thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint,prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank,thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy,thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray,cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable,thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain,thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree};
  438: its linear Pisot specialization is
  439: \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity,cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}.
  440: The eventual-sofic exclusion is recorded only as the brief consequence
  441: \Cref{rem:zeckendorf-primes-not-sofic}, while
  442: \suppref{Theorem~A.1} and \suppref{Proposition~A.2}
  443: remain classical background.
  444: 
  445: \medskip
  446: Finite-automata non-recognizability of the base-\(b\) prime language
  447: goes back to Minsky and Papert \cite{MinskyPapert1966}.
  448: Allen \cite{Allen1968}, Hartmanis--Shank
  449: \cite{HartmanisShank1968}, and Sch\"utzenberger
  450: \cite{Schutzenberger1968} proved stronger related results for broader
  451: language classes and acceptable sets. Shallit's survey and monograph
  452: treat automaticity and number theory from the finite-automata viewpoint
  453: \cite{Shallit1996,AlloucheShallit2003}. Recent work of Yuen and Dubbe
  454: studies regularity and quantitative automaticity around the prime set
  455: \cite{Yuen2022,Dubbe2024}, and Shen proves that prime automata in Yao's
  456: finite-automata primeness model do not exist \cite{Shen2022}. Those
  457: results concern
  458: recognizability or growing-state quantitative automaticity. The present
  459: theorems are different: the automaton is fixed, the comparison is made
  460: on each fixed length slice, and the conclusion is a recall/precision
  461: or symmetric-difference obstruction rather than a state lower bound for

 succeeded in 194ms:
  301: \[
  302:   \{(n+q\ZZ)\cap\NN_{\ge1}:n\ge1,\ q\ge1,\ \gcd(q,a_0)=1\}.
  303: \]
  304: Its completion is
  305: \[
  306:   \widehat{\ZZ}_{S^c}
  307:     :=\varprojlim_{\gcd(q,a_0)=1}\ZZ/q\ZZ
  308:     \cong\prod_{p\notin S}\ZZ_p.
  309: \]
  310: These are the adic topologies and completions studied by Broughan
  311: \cite{Broughan2003}.
  312: 
  313: \begin{theorem}[MCFL local-adic topological fingerprint]
  314:   \label{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}
  315:   For the orbit \(Y=\{N(t):t\ge0\}\) supplied by
  316:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, the following hold.
  317:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  318:     \item The subspace \(Y\subseteq(\NN_{\ge1},\tau_S)\) has no isolated
  319:     points and is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb Q\).
  320:     \item Its closure in \(\widehat{\ZZ}_{S^c}\) is homeomorphic to the
  321:     Cantor set.
  322:     \item If \(B\subseteq\NN_{\ge1}\) is scattered in \(\tau_S\), then
  323:     \[
  324:       \operatorname{Rep}_U(B)
  325:         :=\{w\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(w)\in B\}
  326:     \]
  327:     is MCF-immune whenever it is infinite.
  328:   \end{enumerate}
  329: \end{theorem}
  330: 
  331: \begin{proof}
  332:   Let \(N(t)\in Y\), and let its basic neighborhood be specified modulo
  333:   an allowed \(q\). If \(q=1\), take any later orbit point. If \(q\ge2\),
  334:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit} gives
  335:   \(N(t+H(q))\equiv N(t)\pmod q\), and strict increase makes these points
  336:   distinct. Thus \(Y\) has no isolated point.
  337: 
  338:   The allowed congruences separate distinct positive integers: for
  339:   \(m\ne n\), choose a prime outside the finite set \(S\) that does not
  340:   divide \(m-n\). Consequently \(\tau_S\) is Hausdorff and metrizable;
  341:   it also has a countable basis. Hence \(Y\) is a countable metrizable
  342:   space without isolated points. The Sierpi\'nski characterization used
  343:   in \cite[Theorem~2.4]{Broughan2003} yields \(Y\cong\mathbb Q\).
  344: 
  345:   The profinite ring \(\widehat{\ZZ}_{S^c}\) is compact, metrizable, and
  346:   zero-dimensional. Its closed subspace \(\overline Y\) has no isolated
  347:   point: an isolated point of the closure would, by density of \(Y\),
  348:   belong to and be isolated in \(Y\). Thus \(\overline Y\) is a nonempty
  349:   compact perfect zero-dimensional metrizable space, and the classical
  350:   Cantor-space characterization gives the second assertion; compare
  351:   \cite[Corollary~3.1]{Broughan2003}.
  352: 
  353:   For the last assertion, an infinite MCFL sublanguage of
  354:   \(\operatorname{Rep}_U(B)\) would, by the first assertion, provide a
  355:   nonempty subspace \(Y\subseteq B\) without isolated points. This
  356:   contradicts scatteredness, which is hereditary to subspaces.
  357: \end{proof}
  358: 
  359: For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(n)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(n\),
  360: and let \(\omega_{S^c}(n)=\#\{p\notin S:p\mid n\}\).
  361: For \(K\ge0\) and \(E=(E_p)_{p\in S}\in\NN_0^S\), define
  362: \[
  363:   X_{K,E}=\{n\ge1:\omega_{S^c}(n)\le K,
  364:                \ v_p(n)\le E_p\ (p\in S)\}.
  365: \]
  366: For \(X\subseteq\NN_{\ge1}\), let \(D_SX\) be the set of points of \(X\)
  367: that are not isolated in its \(\tau_S\)-subspace topology. Thus \(D_S\)
  368: is the intrinsic Cantor--Bendixson derivative.
  369: 
  370: \begin{proposition}[Exact local prime-factor rank]
  371:   \label{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}
  372:   For every \(K\ge1\),
  373:   \[
  374:     D_SX_{K,E}=X_{K-1,E}.
  375:   \]
  376:   Consequently
  377:   \[
  378:     D_S^{\,j}X_{K,E}=X_{K-j,E}\quad(0\le j\le K),
  379:     \qquad D_S^{\,K+1}X_{K,E}=\varnothing,
  380:   \]
  381:   and the Cantor--Bendixson height of \(X_{K,E}\) is exactly \(K+1\).
  382: \end{proposition}
  383: 
  384: \begin{proof}
  385:   Suppose first that \(n\in X_{K-1,E}\), and let \(q\ge1\) be coprime
  386:   to \(a_0\). Dirichlet's theorem supplies a prime
  387:   \(r\equiv1\pmod q\) outside the finite set \(S\cup\{p:p\mid n\}\).
  388:   Then \(nr\ne n\), \(nr\equiv n\pmod q\), the \(S\)-adic valuations
  389:   are unchanged, and
  390:   \[
  391:     \omega_{S^c}(nr)=\omega_{S^c}(n)+1\le K.
  392:   \]
  393:   Hence \(n\in D_SX_{K,E}\).
  394: 
  395:   Conversely, let \(n\in X_{K,E}\) have
  396:   \(\omega_{S^c}(n)=K\), and write
  397:   \[
  398:     n=c\prod_{i=1}^K\ell_i^{e_i},
  399:     \qquad c=\prod_{p\in S}p^{f_p},\quad 0\le f_p\le E_p,
  400:   \]
  401:   with distinct \(\ell_i\notin S\). Put
  402:   \(q_0=\prod_i\ell_i^{e_i+1}\). If \(m\in X_{K,E}\) and
  403:   \(m\equiv n\pmod {q_0}\), then
  404:   \(v_{\ell_i}(m)=e_i\) for every \(i\). The budget of \(K\) primes
  405:   outside \(S\) leaves no further such prime, so \(m\) belongs to the
  406:   finite set
  407:   \[
  408:     F=\left\{
  409:       \left(\prod_{p\in S}p^{g_p}\right)
  410:       \prod_{i=1}^K\ell_i^{e_i}:
  411:       0\le g_p\le E_p
  412:     \right\}.
  413:   \]
  414:   Choose a prime \(r\notin S\cup\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_K\}\) dividing
  415:   none of the finitely many nonzero differences \(m-n\), \(m\in F\).
  416:   Then \(q=q_0r\) is coprime to \(a_0\), and the \(q\)-neighborhood of
  417:   \(n\) meets \(X_{K,E}\) only at \(n\). Thus precisely the points with
  418:   fewer than \(K\) outside primes survive one derivative. Iteration
  419:   proves the formula. Finally \(X_{0,E}\) is a nonempty finite set (it
  420:   contains \(1\)), so the height is exactly \(K+1\).
  421: \end{proof}
  422: 
  423: Broughan's related full-adic result counts prime factors with
  424: multiplicity and identifies closures of the corresponding strata
  425: \cite[Theorem~4.3]{Broughan2003}. The preceding proposition instead
  426: uses distinct prime support, deletes the finite set \(S\), imposes
  427: bounded \(S\)-adic valuations, and computes the intrinsic derivative
  428: rank.
  429: 
  430: \begin{theorem}[Nonunit escape dichotomy and MCF-immunity]
  431:   \label{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}
  432:   Let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an infinite MCFL. Then either
  433:   \[
  434:     \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S^c}(\val_U(w))=\infty,
  435:   \]
  436:   or there is a prime \(p\mid a_0\) such that
  437:   \[
  438:     \sup_{w\in L}v_p(\val_U(w))=\infty.
  439:   \]
  440:   Consequently the following languages are MCF-immune whenever they are
  441:   infinite:
  442:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  443:     \item the prime representation language \(\mathcal P_U\);
  444:     \item every language on which \(\Omega(\val_U(w))\) is bounded;
  445:     \item every finite-prime-support language on which all
  446:     \(v_p(\val_U(w))\), \(p\mid a_0\), are bounded.
  447:   \end{enumerate}
  448:   In a unit system, every bounded-\(\omega(\val_U(w))\) language is
  449:   MCF-immune.
  450: \end{theorem}
  451: 
  452: \begin{proof}
  453:   If neither alternative held, finiteness of \(S\) would give
  454:   \(K\ge0\) and \(E\in\NN_0^S\) such that
  455:   \[
  456:     \{\val_U(w):w\in L\}\subseteq X_{K,E}.
  457:   \]
  458:   By \Cref{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}, \(X_{K,E}\) is scattered.
  459:   This contradicts
  460:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}. Prime values satisfy
  461:   \(\omega_{S^c}\le1\) and \(v_p\le1\); bounded \(\Omega\) bounds both
  462:   alternatives; and finite prime support bounds \(\omega_{S^c}\), with
  463:   the remaining valuations bounded by hypothesis. If \(S=\varnothing\),
  464:   the second alternative is absent, giving the unit-system assertion.
  465: \end{proof}
  466: 
  467: The second alternative is necessary. In ordinary base \(b\), where
  468: \(a_0=b\), the regular LSD-first language
  469: \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\) represents \(b^n\). Its distinct prime support is
  470: fixed, while \(v_p(b^n)\) is unbounded for every \(p\mid b\).
  471: 
  472: \begin{proposition}[Recurrence-witness inflation and strict separation]
  473:   \label{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}
  474:   If a tail has minimal recurrence polynomial \(\mu_U\), then for every
  475:   prime \(p\) it also has a recurrence witness with characteristic
  476:   polynomial \((X-p)\mu_U(X)\).  When \(\abs{\mu_U(0)}=1\), the trailing
  477:   coefficient of this witness has absolute value \(p\).
  478: 
  479:   Moreover, there are two canonical eventually recurrent
  480:   numeration systems with regular representation languages and recurrence
  481:   witnesses whose trailing-coefficient prime set is \(\{p\}\), but with
  482:   opposite bounded-outside-prime escape behavior:
  483:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  484:     \item ordinary base \(p\) contains the infinite regular language
  485:     \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\), whose values are \(p^n\);
  486:     \item the Zeckendorf system, equipped with the order-three recurrence
  487:     witness
  488:     \[
  489:       F_{n+3}=-pF_n+(1-p)F_{n+1}+(p+1)F_{n+2},
  490:     \]
  491:     contains no infinite MCFL \(L\) for which
  492:     \[
  493:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{\{p\}^c}(\val(w))<\infty.
  494:     \]
  495:   \end{enumerate}
  496:   Thus the prime divisors of an arbitrarily selected trailing coefficient
  497:   do not determine the escape behavior of the numeration system.
  498: \end{proposition}
  499: 
  500: \begin{proof}
  501:   The polynomial identity \(\mu_U(C)z_J=0\) remains valid after
  502:   multiplication by \(X-p\).  In the companion convention, the trailing
  503:   recurrence coefficient is the negative of the constant term of the
  504:   characteristic polynomial, proving the first assertion.
  505: 
  506:   The base-\(p\) assertion is the preceding example.  For the Zeckendorf
  507:   sequence, multiplication of its minimal polynomial by \(X-p\) gives
  508:   \[
  509:     (X-p)(X^2-X-1)
  510:       =X^3-(p+1)X^2+(p-1)X+p,
  511:   \]
  512:   which is exactly the displayed recurrence and has trailing coefficient
  513:   \(-p\).  This changes neither the sequence nor its regular canonical
  514:   representation language.  On the other hand, its minimal recurrence
  515:   has unit trailing coefficient.  If the displayed supremum were bounded
  516:   by \(K\), then
  517:   \(\omega(\val(w))\le K+1\) on \(L\), contrary to the unit-recurrence
  518:   conclusion of
  519:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}.  This proves the separation.
  520: \end{proof}
  521: 
  761:   \]
  762:   If \(M_i\) is divisible by every prime at most \(B_i\), then every
  763:   prime divisor of \(Q_i\) exceeds \(B_i\).
  764: \end{theorem}
  765: 
  766: \begin{proof}
  767:   Take the fixed orbit \(N(t)\) from
  768:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, discarding finitely many
  769:   initial parameters so that \(N(t)\ge2\). Having selected
  770:   \(N_i=N(t_i)\), apply the synchronized congruence with
  771:   \[
  772:     q_i=M_iN_i^{r_i+1}.
  773:   \]
  774:   Set \(t_{i+1}=t_i+H(q_i)\). Strict increase and the congruence give
  775:   \[
  776:     N_{i+1}=N_i+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i+1}
  777:            =N_i(1+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i})
  778:   \]
  779:   for an integer \(c_i\ge1\). This proves the first assertion. Under
  780:   the last hypothesis, \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod p\) for every prime
  781:   \(p\le B_i\), so none of those primes divides \(Q_i\).
  782: \end{proof}
  783: 
  784: \begin{theorem}[Induced full divisibility tree]
  785:   \label{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}
  786:   Under the hypotheses of
  787:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}, there is an injection
  788:   \[
  789:     \Phi:\NN^{<\omega}\longrightarrow L
  790:   \]
  791:   such that
  792:   \[
  793:     \val_U(\Phi(\sigma))\mid\val_U(\Phi(\tau))
  794:       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma\preceq\tau,
  795:   \]
  796:   where \(\preceq\) denotes the prefix order. The quotients attached to
  797:   distinct edges can be chosen pairwise coprime. Moreover, given an
  798:   arbitrary prescribed threshold for each edge, every prime divisor of
  799:   its quotient can be required to exceed that threshold.
  800: \end{theorem}
  801: 
  802: \begin{proof}
  803:   Use the fixed strictly increasing orbit from
  804:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}. Enumerate the edges of
  805:   \(\NN^{<\omega}\) so that each parent occurs before its children. Map
  806:   the root to any orbit word of value \(R_0\ge2\). Suppose finitely many
  807:   edges have been assigned, and consider a new edge from a parent of
  808:   value \(P\). Let \(R\) be divisible by \(R_0\), by every previously
  809:   assigned edge quotient, and by every prime not exceeding the prescribed
  810:   threshold for the new edge. Apply the synchronized orbit congruence
  811:   modulo \(P^2R\) at the parameter of the parent. A sufficiently large
  812:   positive multiple of the return time gives an unused orbit word of
  813:   value \(P'>P\) with
  814:   \[
  815:     P'\equiv P\pmod {P^2R}.
  816:   \]
  817:   Hence \(P'=PQ\), where \(Q>1\) and \(Q\equiv1\pmod {PR}\). In
  818:   particular, \(Q\) is coprime to the root and to every earlier edge
  819:   quotient, and no prime up to the prescribed threshold divides \(Q\).
  820: 
  821:   Recursion defines \(\Phi\) on every node. The value at a node is the
  822:   root value times the product of the edge quotients along its path.
  823:   Since the root and all distinct edge quotients are pairwise coprime,
  824:   a node value divides another exactly when its path-edge set is an
  825:   initial segment of the other path. This is precisely the prefix
  826:   relation and also proves injectivity.
  827: \end{proof}
  828: 
  829: \begin{theorem}[Prime immunity for recurrent numeration systems]
  830:   \label{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}
  831:   Let \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\) satisfy \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, and put
  832:   \[
  833:     \mathcal P_U
  834:       :=\{w\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(w)\text{ is prime}\}.
  835:   \]
  836:   Then \(\mathcal P_U\) is MCF-immune, and therefore CF-immune,
  837:   REG-immune, and not recognizable by a finite automaton over \(A\).
  838: 
  839:   If, in addition, \(\abs{a_0}=1\), then every infinite multiple
  840:   context-free
  841:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
  842:   \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
  843:   coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
  844:   \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
  845:   bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
  846:   system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
  847:   hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
  848: \end{theorem}
  849: 
  850: \begin{proof}
  851:   The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
  852:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
  853:   bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
  854:   that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
  855:   \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
  856:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
  857:   Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
  858:   MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
  859:   \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
  860: \end{proof}
  861: 
  862: \begin{corollary}[Linear Pisot \(U\)-systems]
  863:   \label{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}
  864:   Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a linear Pisot \(U\)-system in the
  865:   following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly increasing
  866:   integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  867:   reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  868:   eventually satisfies an integral recurrence whose characteristic
  869:   polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a Pisot number. Then its prime
  870:   representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  871:   nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  872:   convention.
  873: 
  874:   If the dominant Pisot number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  875:   trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  876:   bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  877:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
  878: \end{corollary}
  879: 
  880: \begin{proof}
  881:   Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  882:   integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  883:   place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)--(U3)} hold. The defining
  884:   Pisot recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  885:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. Frougny's finite
  886:   normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer for normalization
  887:   in this Pisot setting, and the associated canonical syntax and
  888:   Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  889:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  890:   Those finite-state results identify this corollary with the usual
  891:   recognizability convention; the immunity proof itself uses only
  892:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}. Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  893:   regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  894:   convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  895:   conclusion.
  896: \end{proof}
  897: 
  898: \begin{example}[Unit and nonunit Pisot systems]
  899:   \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
  900:   The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
  901:   \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
  902:   Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
  903:   coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
  904:   ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
  905:   follows, recovering the classical conclusion, but the unit iteration
  906:   is not being asserted. A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example
  907:   is the dominant root \(1+\sqrt3\) of \(X^2-2X-2\): the recurrence
  908:   \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n\) has \(a_0=2\), and the action is singular
  909:   modulo \(2\).
  910: \end{example}
  911: 
  912: \begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
  913:   \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
  914:   The terminology for Pisot numeration systems is not uniform.
  915:   \Cref{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity} covers the standard
  916:   positional linear \(U\)-systems just specified, including integer
  917:   bases, Zeckendorf/Fibonacci, Pell, and higher-order Pisot recurrences.
  918:   It does not assert the theorem for arbitrary real-base
  919:   \(\beta\)-shift representations, non-positional abstract numeration
  920:   systems, redundant noninjective digit systems, or systems lacking an
  921:   eventual integral recurrence and strict length ordering. Extending
  922:   the argument to any of those classes requires a stationary finite
  923:   block action that is invertible modulo represented primes.
  924: 
  925:   For a fixed nonunit recurrence witness, the ambient action can be
  926:   singular modulo primes dividing \(a_0\), so the unrestricted unit-system
  927:   divisibility tree need not follow. The witness-relative surviving
  928:   statement is \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}: every infinite
  929:   MCFL must acquire unbounded prime support outside that finite set or
  930:   unbounded valuation at one of its primes. The invariant restricted
  931:   action and the failure of arbitrary recurrence witnesses to classify
  932:   escape behavior are distinguished in
  933:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}.
  934:   The ordinary-base example preceding
  935:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} shows that the valuation
  936:   alternative cannot be removed.
  937: \end{remark}

# Literature and Novelty Check

Checked on 2026-08-02.  The arXiv searches below used the public Atom API
endpoint `https://export.arxiv.org/api/query`; DOI metadata was checked against
the Crossref REST API.  The purpose of the search was to delimit the theorem
claims, not to infer novelty from a null keyword search.

## arXiv API queries

The following literal `search_query` values were sent to the API (20 results
maximum per query):

- `all:"context-free" AND all:prime AND all:language`: four returned records,
  none on prime numeration languages.  The only mathematically related record
  was Borchert--Rampersad, *Inverse Star, Borders, and Palstars*,
  arXiv:1008.2440; it does not concern prime recognizability.
- `all:Pisot AND all:numeration AND all:automata`: eight returned records,
  including Carton--Couvreur--Delacourt--Ollinger,
  *Linear Recurrence Sequence Automata and the Addition of Abstract Numeration
  Systems*, arXiv:2406.09868 (conference DOI
  10.1007/978-3-031-97548-6_7); Charlier--Cisternino--Stipulanti,
  *Robustness of Pisot-regular sequences*, arXiv:2006.11126,
  DOI 10.1016/j.aam.2020.102151; Massuir--Peltomaki--Rigo,
  *Automatic sequences based on Parry or Bertrand numeration systems*,
  arXiv:1810.11081, DOI 10.1016/j.aam.2019.03.003; and
  Frougny--Steiner, *Minimal weight expansions in Pisot bases*,
  arXiv:0803.2874, DOI 10.1515/JMC.2008.017.  None of the returned records
  states prime-language REG- or CF-immunity.
- `all:"prime language" AND all:automata`: no returned records.
- `all:"abstract numeration systems" AND all:prime`: no returned records.
- `all:Ogden AND all:"interchange lemma"`: no returned records.  These are
  pre-arXiv classical papers and are cited by DOI below.
- Exact-title queries confirmed Dubbe, *The automaticity of the set of
  primes*, arXiv:2409.04314, DOI 10.1016/j.tcs.2025.115480, and Yuen,
  *Kleene Star of the Primes is not Regular in Any Base*, arXiv:2203.16088.

The arXiv API search is negative evidence only.  In particular, the older
JACM papers settle a stronger fixed-base question than their titles alone
suggest, so the paper does not advertise fixed-base CF-immunity as new.

## Exact classical citations

- William Ogden, "A helpful result for proving inherent ambiguity,"
  *Mathematical Systems Theory* 2 (1968), 191--194,
  DOI 10.1007/BF01694004.  This is the marked-position pumping lemma now
  called Ogden's lemma.
- William Ogden, Rockford J. Ross, and Karl Winklmann, "An 'Interchange
  Lemma' for Context-Free Languages," *SIAM Journal on Computing* 14 (1985),
  410--415, DOI 10.1137/0214031.  The present proof does not claim or reproduce
  their interchange lemma; ordinary context-free pumping suffices after a
  fixed-prefix quotient, while Ogden's lemma gives an alternative way to
  localize pumping beyond an eventual-recurrence transient.
- J. Hartmanis and H. Shank, "On the Recognition of Primes by Automata,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 15 (1968), 382--389,
  DOI 10.1145/321466.321470.
- M. P. Schutzenberger, "A Remark on Acceptable Sets of Numbers,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 15 (1968), 300--303,
  DOI 10.1145/321450.321461.  Contemporary citation records describe the
  Hartmanis--Shank and Schutzenberger conclusion as: no infinite set of
  base-`b` primes is recognized by a finite automaton or a pushdown automaton.
  Thus fixed-base prime CF-immunity is prior art.
- M. Minsky and S. Papert, "Unrecognizable Sets of Numbers,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 13 (1966), 281--286,
  DOI 10.1145/321328.321337.
- D. P. Allen, Jr., "On a characterization of the nonregular set of primes,"
  *Journal of Computer and System Sciences* 2 (1968), 464--467,
  DOI 10.1016/S0022-0000(68)80038-8.

## Pisot and numeration references

- Christiane Frougny, "Representations of numbers and finite automata,"
  *Mathematical Systems Theory* 25 (1992), 37--60,
  DOI 10.1007/BF01368783.  This is the normalization/finite-transducer source
  used for linear numeration systems whose characteristic polynomial has the
  Pisot property.
- Veronique Bruyere and Georges Hansel, "Bertrand numeration systems and
  recognizability," *Theoretical Computer Science* 181 (1997), 17--43,
  DOI 10.1016/S0304-3975(96)00260-5.
- Christiane Frougny and Boris Solomyak, "Finite beta-expansions,"
  *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* 12 (1992), 713--723,
  DOI 10.1017/S0143385700007057.
- Stephane Fabre, "Substitutions et beta-systemes de numeration,"
  *Theoretical Computer Science* 137 (1995), 219--236,
  DOI 10.1016/0304-3975(95)91132-A.
- P. B. A. Lecomte and M. Rigo, "Numeration Systems on a Regular Language,"
  *Theory of Computing Systems* 34 (2001), 27--44,
  DOI 10.1007/S002240010014.  This is cited to distinguish abstract
  numeration systems from the narrower linear Pisot `U`-systems proved here.

## Novelty boundary used in the manuscript

The following assertions are treated as new only relative to the literature
located above and are stated with their full hypotheses:

1. The two-pump block-action congruence modulo the square of the represented
   value and the resulting coprime-quotient chain for an arbitrary
   context-free sublanguage of canonical Zeckendorf representations.
2. CF-immunity of the Zeckendorf prime language, and the stronger unbounded
   distinct-prime-divisor consequences for context-free Zeckendorf
   sublanguages.
3. Prime REG- and CF-immunity for the explicitly defined class of positional
   linear Pisot `U`-systems: integer weights, finite digit alphabet, injective
   canonical representations ordered by length, and an eventual integral
   recurrence with nonzero trailing coefficient.  The proof uses only the
   recurrence block action; Frougny normalization supplies the standard
   finite-state canonical syntax/normalization interface for Pisot
   `U`-systems.

No claim is made for every object sometimes called a "Pisot numeration
system."  In particular, arbitrary real-base beta-shifts, non-positional
abstract numeration systems, systems without an eventual integral recurrence,
and non-injective redundant representations are explicit open interfaces.
The Pisot-unit hypothesis is needed for the unrestricted deep-quotient and
induced-tree conclusions and for unconditional bounded-omega immunity. For a
nonunit recurrence, primes dividing the trailing coefficient make the
companion action singular modulo some composite values. The local-adic
dichotomy nevertheless gives prime and bounded-Omega MCF-immunity; bounded
distinct-prime support can escape only through unbounded valuation at a prime
dividing the trailing coefficient.

## Multiple-context-free and adic extension (2026-08-03)

The public arXiv Atom endpoint at https://export.arxiv.org/api/query was queried
with the following literal searches (and with a single-record
search_query=id:2509.02117 control):

- all:"multiple context-free" AND all:pumping;
- all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime;
- all:"adic topology" AND all:integers;
- all:"Cantor-Bendixson" AND all:"prime factors";
- all:"divisibility tree" AND all:language.

Every API request returned HTTP 429 after retries with an identifying user
agent and four-second spacing. These failures are not treated as null search
results. The corresponding arXiv web searches, Crossref bibliographic
searches, DBLP metadata, and exact-source checks located no paper asserting an
MCFL prime-immunity theorem for recurrence numeration, an MCFL-induced local
congruence orbit, or the induced divisibility-tree conclusion.

The following published inputs delimit what is not new:

- H. Seki, T. Matsumura, M. Fujii, and T. Kasami, "On multiple
  context-free grammars," *Theoretical Computer Science* 88 (1991),
  191--229, DOI 10.1016/0304-3975(91)90374-B. Its Lemma 3.2 is the weak
  pumping lemma supplying one synchronized family with 2k pumped factors.
- M. Kanazawa, G. M. Kobele, J. Michaelis, S. Salvati, and R. Yoshinaka,
  "The Failure of the Strong Pumping Lemma for Multiple Context-Free
  Languages," *Theory of Computing Systems* 55 (2014), 250--278,
  DOI 10.1007/S00224-014-9534-Z.
- A. Duncan, M. Elder, L. Frenkel, and M. Liu, "A substitution lemma for
  multiple context-free languages," *International Journal of Algebra and
  Computation* (2026), DOI 10.1142/S0218196726500463,
  arXiv:2509.02117. The direct arXiv PDF was checked; its Lemma 5.3 quotes
  the exact Seki weak-pumping factorization used in the manuscript.
- K. A. Broughan, "Adic Topologies for the Rational Integers," *Canadian
  Journal of Mathematics* 55 (2003), 711--723,
  DOI 10.4153/CJM-2003-030-3. The Cambridge primary PDF was checked.
  Theorem 2.4 gives the rational-space classification, Corollary 3.1 gives
  the Cantor completion, and Theorem 4.3 treats full-adic prime-factor
  strata counted with multiplicity.

Accordingly, the manuscript cites the Seki pumping family and Broughan's
topological classifications as inputs. The claims retained as new are the
combination with a fixed recurrence block orbit, the deleted-prime intrinsic
Cantor--Bendixson rank for distinct prime support with bounded local
valuations, the nonunit escape dichotomy and MCF-immunity consequences, and
the unit-system arbitrary-depth quotient and induced-tree constructions.

## Geometric-ray characterization (2026-08-07)

The public arXiv Atom API returned zero records for each of the following
literal queries:

- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"linear recurrence"\`;

- \`all:"Pisot numeration" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"numeration system" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"linear MCFG" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"semidecidable" AND all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"numeration"\`.

Crossref and OpenAlex searches for the corresponding unquoted combinations
returned general references on MCFGs, geometric-progression-free sets, and
Pisot numeration, but no work combining an MCFL sublanguage, bounded prime
support, and an exact geometric numerical ray. This is negative novelty
evidence only.

Two published inputs delimit the claim. Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami,
*Theoretical Computer Science* 88 (1991), 191--229, supply the weak
synchronized pumping family. J.-H. Evertse, "On sums of \(S\)-units and
linear recurrences," *Compositio Mathematica* 53 (1984), 225--244,
Theorem 3, proves unbounded prime-ideal support in ratios of terms of a
nondegenerate recurrence with at least two characteristic roots. The latter
excludes a fixed-\(S\)-unit nondegenerate subsequence; Schur's polynomial
prime-divisor theorem handles the remaining one-root polynomial factor.
Neither published input states the manuscript's equivalence with the
existence of a finite-fan-out synchronized MCFG ray, nor the resulting
positive-semidecidability statement.

  841:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
  842:   \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
  843:   coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
  844:   \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
  845:   bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
  846:   system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
  847:   hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
  848: \end{theorem}
  849: 
  850: \begin{proof}
  851:   The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
  852:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
  853:   bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
  854:   that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
  855:   \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
  856:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
  857:   Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
  858:   MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
  859:   \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
  860: \end{proof}

  862: \begin{corollary}[Linear Pisot \(U\)-systems]
  863:   \label{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}
  864:   Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a linear Pisot \(U\)-system in the
  865:   following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly increasing
  866:   integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  867:   reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  868:   eventually satisfies an integral recurrence whose characteristic
  869:   polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a Pisot number. Then its prime
  870:   representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  871:   nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  872:   convention.
  873: 
  874:   If the dominant Pisot number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  875:   trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  876:   bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  877:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
  878: \end{corollary}
  879: 
  880: \begin{proof}
  881:   Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  882:   integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  883:   place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)--(U3)} hold. The defining
  884:   Pisot recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  885:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. Frougny's finite
  886:   normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer for normalization
  887:   in this Pisot setting, and the associated canonical syntax and
  888:   Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  889:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  890:   Those finite-state results identify this corollary with the usual
  891:   recognizability convention; the immunity proof itself uses only
  892:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}. Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  893:   regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  894:   convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  895:   conclusion.
  896: \end{proof}

  898: \begin{example}[Unit and nonunit Pisot systems]
  899:   \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
  900:   The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
  901:   \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
  902:   Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
  903:   coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
  904:   ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
  905:   follows, recovering the classical conclusion, but the unit iteration
  906:   is not being asserted. A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example
  907:   is the dominant root \(1+\sqrt3\) of \(X^2-2X-2\): the recurrence
  908:   \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n\) has \(a_0=2\), and the action is singular
  909:   modulo \(2\).
  910: \end{example}

  912: \begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
  913:   \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
  914:   The terminology for Pisot numeration systems is not uniform.
  915:   \Cref{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity} covers the standard
  916:   positional linear \(U\)-systems just specified, including integer
  917:   bases, Zeckendorf/Fibonacci, Pell, and higher-order Pisot recurrences.
  918:   It does not assert the theorem for arbitrary real-base
  919:   \(\beta\)-shift representations, non-positional abstract numeration
  920:   systems, redundant noninjective digit systems, or systems lacking an
  921:   eventual integral recurrence and strict length ordering. Extending
  922:   the argument to any of those classes requires a stationary finite
  923:   block action that is invertible modulo represented primes.
  924: 
  925:   For a fixed nonunit recurrence witness, the ambient action can be
  926:   singular modulo primes dividing \(a_0\), so the unrestricted unit-system
  927:   divisibility tree need not follow. The witness-relative surviving
  928:   statement is \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}: every infinite
  929:   MCFL must acquire unbounded prime support outside that finite set or
  930:   unbounded valuation at one of its primes. The invariant restricted
  931:   action and the failure of arbitrary recurrence witnesses to classify
  932:   escape behavior are distinguished in
  933:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}.
  934:   The ordinary-base example preceding
  935:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} shows that the valuation
  936:   alternative cannot be removed.
  937: \end{remark}

  366: \smallskip
  367: \noindent\textbf{Relation to density and approximation literature.} For ordinary
  368: automatic sets, asymptotic density questions go back at least to
  369: Berstel \cite{Berstel1973}; the standard global sources include
  370: B\"uchi's automata-theoretic decidability work \cite{Buchi1960} and
  371: Allouche--Shallit's monograph on automatic sequences
  372: \cite{AlloucheShallit2003}. Matrix and algorithmic treatments appear
  373: in
  374: \cite{BodirskyGaertnerVonOertzenSchwinghammer2004,Bell2020UpperDensity},
  375: and Koga's paper \cite{Koga2019Density} revisits Sin'ya's density-zero
  376: criterion \cite{Sinya2021}. The rational-measure viewpoint of Hansel
  377: and Perrin \cite{HanselPerrin1989} interprets regular languages via
  378: probability measures on shifts of finite type. Kozik's MFCS 2005 paper
  379: \cite{Kozik2005Conditional} formulates conditional densities for
  380: deterministic presentations in the trim strongly connected setting,
  381: Montoya \cite{Montoya2025Relative} recasts these questions in terms of
  382: relative densities, and Berth\'e--Goulet-Ouellet--Perrin
  383: \cite{BertheGouletPerrin2025} establish a broad density theorem under
  384: shift-invariant measures. Accordingly,
  385: \suppref{Theorem~1.2}, \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-powerlaw}, and
  386: \suppref{Theorem~1.18}
  387: should be read here as background statements in a form suited to the
  388: prime-slice applications, while
  389: \suppref{Theorem~1.14} is the exponent-sensitive
  390: extension needed for general trim deterministic presentations. Cobham's
  391: theorem
  392: \cite{Cobham1969} is the foundational reference for base-dependent
  393: automatic recognizability of sets of integers. Regular approximation of
  394: non-regular languages is a separate line of work; see, for example,
  395: Eisman and Ravikumar \cite{EismanRavikumar2005} and the asymptotic
  396: approximation framework of Sin'ya \cite{Sinya2021}. Polynomial and
  397: sparse growth phenomena for regular languages are part of the classical
  398: transfer-matrix picture \cite{Berstel1973,SalomaaSoittola1978}, and
  399: numeration systems on regular languages are treated in
  400: \cite{LecomteRigo2001,Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,CharlierRampersad2011,Rigo2014Vol1,Rigo2014Vol2}.
  401: The present contribution is narrower: it packages the fixed-DFA
  402: prime-slice obstruction with computable residue-class constants and
  403: explicit thresholds, then applies the same finite-budget argument in the
  404: Zeckendorf setting.
  405: 
  406: 
  407: \medskip
  408: \noindent\textbf{Summary.} \suppref{Theorem~1.2 and Lemma~1.16} and
  409: \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-powerlaw}
  410: record the density statements needed for deterministic presentations.
  411: \suppref{Theorem~1.14} gives the general trim
  412: deterministic finite-budget theorem, including multiple maximal
  413: components, Perron-active residue classes, and their polynomial factors,
  414: and \suppref{Theorem~1.18} records the strongly connected
  415: specialization used for Zeckendorf. The paper's effective contribution
  416: is the finite-budget obstruction mechanism with quantitative fixed-DFA
  417: recall/precision and symmetric-difference instances; see
  418: \suppref{Corollary~1.19}, \suppref{Proposition~1.9},
  419: \suppref{Corollary~1.10}, and \suppref{Corollary~1.12}.
  420: The Zeckendorf analogues are
  421: \Cref{cor:zeck-symmetric-diff,cor:zeck-recall-precision}. The
  422: Zeckendorf prime-language theorem is downstream of the PNT-free
  423: coprime-quotient pumping theorem
  424: \Cref{thm:coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. Its principal
  425: consequences are
  426: \Cref{cor:unbounded-distinct-prime-divisors,cor:bounded-distinct-prime-zeckendorf-languages-reg-immune}
  427: and \Cref{cor:finite-prime-support-zeckendorf-languages-reg-immune};
  428: \Cref{prop:zeckendorf-regular-slice-rigidity} remains a separate
  429: slice-cardinality obstruction, and
  430: \Cref{cor:zeckendorf-prime-language-not-regular} is an immediate
  431: consequence of REG-immunity.
  432: Context-free Zeckendorf pumping is
  433: \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}, with the
  434: immunity consequences in
  435: \Cref{cor:zeckendorf-context-free-immunity-package}. The stronger MCFL
  436: package is
  437: \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit,thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint,prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank,thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy,thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray,cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable,thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain,thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree};
  438: its linear Pisot specialization is
  439: \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity,cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}.
  440: The eventual-sofic exclusion is recorded only as the brief consequence
  441: \Cref{rem:zeckendorf-primes-not-sofic}, while
  442: \suppref{Theorem~A.1} and \suppref{Proposition~A.2}
  443: remain classical background.
  444: 
  445: \medskip
  446: Finite-automata non-recognizability of the base-\(b\) prime language
  447: goes back to Minsky and Papert \cite{MinskyPapert1966}.
  448: Allen \cite{Allen1968}, Hartmanis--Shank
  449: \cite{HartmanisShank1968}, and Sch\"utzenberger
  450: \cite{Schutzenberger1968} proved stronger related results for broader
  451: language classes and acceptable sets. Shallit's survey and monograph
  521: \cite{HanselPerrin1989,Kozik2005Conditional,Koga2019Density,Montoya2025Relative,BertheGouletPerrin2025}
  522: give the periodic or conditional density statements used here; the new
  523: increment is to feed the resulting residue constants into explicit
  524: prime-slice thresholds for one fixed automaton. Numeration-system work
  525: \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,CharlierRampersad2011,Rigo2014Vol1,Rigo2014Vol2}
  526: supplies regular admissible languages and growth laws for abstract
  527: numeration, including Zeckendorf-type systems; in the trim strongly
  528: connected cases stated explicitly, the present paper transfers the same
  529: fixed-prime-slice obstruction to Zeckendorf length slices with computable
  530: constants. For primes in Fibonacci or Zeckendorf representations, we use
  531: only the prime number theorem estimate
  532: \(\#\{p\in[F_{m+1},F_{m+2})\}\asymp\varphi^m/m\), and no distribution
  533: theorem for Zeckendorf digit patterns is claimed.
  534: 
  535: The sofic and orbit-growth papers
  536: \cite{BustosKellendonkYassawi2025,CharlierCisternino2021}, together with
  537: the classical zeta references recalled in \suppref{Appendix~A}, are used
  538: only for contextual comparison: the present argument separates those
  539: phenomena from the fixed prime-slice density obstruction. Similarly,
  540: regular-approximation frameworks for nonregular languages
  541: \cite{EismanRavikumar2005,Sinya2021} position the problem, but the
  542: obstruction proved here is slice-wise and quantitative for one fixed DFA,
  543: not an optimal approximation scheme. The main theorem chain,
  544: \suppref{Theorem~1.7}, \suppref{Theorem~1.14}, and
  545: \suppref{Corollary~1.19},
  546: computes residue alternatives, thresholds, and constants for a fixed
  547: finite automaton, and compares multicomponent polynomial exponents
  548: against a prime budget of order \(\lambda^m/m\).
  549: 
  550: \subsection{Organisation}
  551: 
  552: \suppref{Section~1} proves the density dichotomy for deterministic
  553: automata and derives the fixed-base prime corollaries.
  554: \Cref{sec:zeckendorf} records the background growth law for regular
  555: Zeckendorf sublanguages, deduces the corresponding quantitative prime
  556: corollaries, proves the PNT-free coprime-quotient Zeckendorf pumping
  557: theorem and its unbounded-\(\omega\), bounded-distinct-prime,
  558: finite-prime-support, and prime-language REG-immunity corollaries,
  559: records the older slice-level
  560: rigidity as a separate density obstruction, and then notes the easy
  561: nonregularity and sofic exclusions.
  562: \Cref{sec:context-free-pisot} proves the paired-pump Zeckendorf theorem,
  563: the synchronized MCFL orbit, its local-adic and Cantor--Bendixson
  564: consequences, the nonunit escape dichotomy, the geometric-ray
  565: characterization and its positive semidecidability consequence, and the
  566: unit-system divisibility tree, then specializes the recurrent interface
  567: to linear Pisot \(U\)-systems.

- `all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime`.

The broader query `all:"Pisot numeration" AND all:prime` returned only
Adrian-Maria Scheerer, "Normality in Pisot Numeration Systems,"
arXiv:1503.08047, published in *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* 37
(2017), 1872--1886, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.53. It concerns normality of
prime concatenations and does not address MCFLs, reachable recurrence
lattices, or recurrence-witness inflation. The query
`all:"minimal polynomial" AND all:"numeration system" AND all:recurrence`
returned only Olivier Carton, Jake Sudbery, and Reem Yassawi, "From some
Pisot numerations to topological groups," arXiv:2606.30496. Its abstract
studies Condition F, topological
groups, and torus factors; it does not state the minimal-reachable determinant
lemma or the base-\(p\)/inflated-Fibonacci escape separation.

The cyclic-subspace identities used in the oracle response---equality of the
minimal and characteristic polynomials on a cyclic restriction, and recovery
of the minimal polynomial from the first Krylov dependence---are standard
rational-canonical-form facts; see F. R. Gantmacher, *The Theory of Matrices*,
vol. I, Chelsea, 1959, Chapter VI. They are not retained as new theorem
content.

Crossref bibliographic searches for `multiple context-free Pisot numeration
prime factor`, `minimal recurrence reachable lattice numeration`, `inflated
Fibonacci recurrence nonunit Pisot`, and `affine semigroup p-adic numeration`
returned only standard Pisot tiling, numeration, recurrence, and affine
semigroup papers unrelated to the retained strict separation. These searches are
negative novelty evidence, not a proof that no related result exists.

## Geometric-ray characterization (2026-08-07)

The public arXiv Atom API returned zero records for each of the following
literal queries:

- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"linear recurrence"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"S-unit"\`;
- \`all:"Pisot numeration" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"numeration system" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"linear MCFG" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"semidecidable" AND all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"numeration"\`.

Crossref and OpenAlex searches for the corresponding unquoted combinations
returned general references on MCFGs, geometric-progression-free sets, and
Pisot numeration, but no work combining an MCFL sublanguage, bounded prime
support, and an exact geometric numerical ray. This is negative novelty
evidence only.

Two published inputs delimit the claim. Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami,
*Theoretical Computer Science* 88 (1991), 191--229, supply the weak
synchronized pumping family. J.-H. Evertse, "On sums of \(S\)-units and
linear recurrences," *Compositio Mathematica* 53 (1984), 225--244,
Theorem 3, proves unbounded prime-ideal support in ratios of terms of a
nondegenerate recurrence with at least two characteristic roots. The latter
excludes a fixed-\(S\)-unit nondegenerate subsequence; Schur's polynomial
prime-divisor theorem handles the remaining one-root polynomial factor.
Neither published input states the manuscript's equivalence with the
existence of a finite-fan-out synchronized MCFG ray, nor the resulting
positive-semidecidability statement.

## Refreshed prior-art and decision-target audit (2026-08-08)

The two referee-critical classical records were rechecked against their
publisher metadata and indexed abstracts, rather than inferred from their
titles. Crossref gives DOI 10.1145/321466.321470 for Hartmanis--Shank and DOI
10.1145/321450.321461 for Schutzenberger. The Hartmanis--Shank abstract states
that neither the primes nor any infinite subset of the primes, in fixed-base
notation, is accepted by a pushdown or finite automaton. The Schutzenberger
abstract states that the two negative results on acceptable sets are extended
to arbitrary context-free languages. CORE's Cornell record reproduces the
Hartmanis--Shank abstract; Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall confirm the records
and publisher copies. The manuscript already cites both papers where it calls
fixed-base prime CF-immunity classical and explicitly says that their proofs
are not reproduced as new.

The reference lists supplied by Crossref were also inspected. They lead to
the already cited Minsky--Papert paper on unrecognizable sets, the classical
context-free-language sources, and the contemporary finite-automata work.
No item in those lists concerns Zeckendorf or Pisot numeration, MCFLs, a
recurrence block action, or the geometric-ray criterion.

A live arXiv API query for `all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime`
returned zero records. Google Scholar searches for `"primes" "multiple
context-free" language`, `"Pisot numeration" prime language automata`, and
`"S-unit" "linear recurrence" geometric progression` returned the standard
MCFG pumping literature, general numeration references, and recurrence/S-unit
sources, but no prime-language result in Pisot numeration. Crossref searches
confirmed the two 1968 JACM papers and their citation trails. A zbMATH API
keyword search for `multiple context-free prime numeration` returned no
record. OpenAlex exhausted its anonymous daily query budget during the audit,
and the first Semantic Scholar search was rate-limited; these failures are
recorded as failures, not as negative results.

The proposed decision target does not define a new problem for the class
proved in the manuscript. Theorem~3.18 proves that the prime representation
language of every system satisfying (U1)--(U4) is MCF-immune, and Euclid's
theorem plus canonical representation makes that language infinite.
Consequently it is never an MCFL. For effectively presented regular canonical
linear Pisot U-systems, the requested terminating algorithm is therefore the
constant algorithm returning `NO`; this is an immediate corollary, not a
tier-raising decision theorem.

The genuinely nontrivial nearby decision problem is whether the bounded-
outside-support condition in Theorem~3.14 holds, equivalently whether a
geometric synchronized scheme exists. Corollary~3.15 gives only positive
semidecidability. A full decision procedure would require an effective finite
bound on the number and lengths of synchronized pumped blocks, or an
equivalent negative certificate for the absence of exact geometric identities
among recurrence sequences generated by finite transition and affine-matrix
semigroups. No such bound follows from the cited pumping or recurrence
theorems; general zero/equality questions for linear recurrences already meet
Skolem-type barriers. The present tools therefore do not justify promoting
that semidecision procedure to a decision theorem.

codex
The candidate set is now broader than the original decision question: besides general decidability, it includes a complete linear-Pisot classification, ratio-prime rigidity, removal of the nonunit valuation escape for irrational Pisot bases, a sharp Cantor–Bendixson contrast when bad-prime valuations are unbounded, and finite-state extensions beyond deterministic presentations. I’m scoring these against live bibliographic APIs now; the most promising proof target is the classification “bounded outside-support MCFL exists iff the Pisot base is an integer.”
